newsitem.title: JAPAN: Prolonged port strike could hurt Japan commodities.
newsitem.headline: Prolonged port strike could hurt Japan commodities.

text.p: Japanese commodity traders said on Thursday they doubted a planned 24-hour port workers' strike next week would affect the markets, although there was potential for disruption if the work stoppage drags on.

Non-ferrous metal traders in particular fretted that large shipments of refined metal imported under a special duty-free scheme and due to arrive in late March would lose their tariff exemptions if unloading were delayed until April.
"If that (24 hours) is all the strike lasts, there won't be any impact, but if a weekday strike becomes long-term, a variety of effects will emerge," said a copper trader at a leading trade house.

On Wednesday two major labour unions decided to stage a 24-hour nationwide strike on March 12 to protest against U.S. and European pressure for Japanese port reforms and to press for better working conditions.
Workers from the two unions will also refuse to handle cargoes on Sundays from March 16 onward, union officials said.
The strike on March 12 would affect operations of container ships docking at all major ports in Japan, including Yokohama and Kobe, a union official said.
Japanese grain market sources saw little need to worry about the strike, unless it turns into a long-term action.
Japan's feed makers currently hold ample stocks of corn and other feed grains and a 24-hour strike would not cause any immediate supply problems, industry officials said.
"I don't think people are worried about it," a corn trader at a major Tokyo-based trade house said. "If it lasts for long, say about a week, then it will make a difference."
Japan is the largest importer of grains, particularly corn and soybeans, from the United States.

The Food Agency of Japan, the country's sole importer of wheat, barley and rice, said its grain discharge operations across the country will be suspended on March 12, although the impact will be limited.
"Our discharge operations will be stopped, but the impact will be limited if they end the strike in 24 hours," said an agency official.
Japan's tyre makers also saw little cause for concern over the strike.
"We have been preparing for the planned action, by changing delivery schedules and so on, so I don't see any significant impact from the strike," an official at a major tyre manufacturer said.
Metal traders, however, said that late March was a particularly touchy time for their markets.
Japan's general system of preferences (GSP) scheme exempts developing-country imports from tariffs if they are submitted for customs clearance by the beginning of the new fiscal year on April 1.

GSP-related shipments of Chinese zinc are expected to be particularly heavy, due to tightness in the domestic market, and an extended strike could delay shipments and force traders and end-users to forfeit the tariff exemption.
"If it becomes a full-fledged strike, it could be tough for us," said one Japanese zinc trader.
